title: Fasting mimicking diet (FMD) in patients with congenital gastrointestinal tumor syndromes (ANTIPASTO-1)
summary:
According to current estimates, more than 300,000 people in Germany have genetic changes that are associated with an increased risk, especially of cancer of the gastrointestinal tract. Only a minority of these high-risk patients are currently identified. These hereditary tumor diseases include Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).
Lynch syndrome is the leading cause of hereditary colorectal cancer and is responsible for approximately 3% of all colorectal cancer cases. Mortality depends on various factors, including the type and stage of the tumor, early detection and treatment, and patient-specific and other genetic influences. Individuals with the genetic predisposition have an 80-90% lifetime risk of developing at least one tumor associated with Lynch syndrome, with intestinal tumors being the most common and having a lifetime risk of 60-70%. Apart from surgical removal of the tumors, there are no therapeutic approaches to prevent cancer development in these patients.
Studies in mice with tumors have shown that periodic fasting or a sham diet (Fasting-Mimicking Diet = FMD) with low carbohydrates and proteins can support the antitumor effects of chemotherapy, immunotherapy or hormone therapies. Based on these preclinical results, clinical trials were initiated to investigate the feasibility and antitumor activity of cyclic FMD in combination with standard tumor therapies in various clinical contexts.
A study with breast cancer patients showed that five-day FMD was safe and easy to perform. Here, FMD was performed every 21 to 28 days in combination with standard cancer treatments and caused a change in the patients' metabolism and immune response to cancer cells. The diet caused relatively few serious side effects in the studies (12.9%). It should also be noted that some of the side effects attributed to the diet (such as fatigue or nausea) could also have been caused by the accompanying cancer therapy.  The diet was adhered to by more than 90% of patients across all diet cycles. An important concern with fasting or fasting-like diets for cancer patients is the risk of increased weight loss. Therefore, patients who were underweight or at risk of malnutrition were excluded. One of the most important discoveries from these studies is the far-reaching effect of the fasting-like diet on the immune system. This diet was found to alter the number of certain immune cells. At the same time, the researchers observed similar and desirable changes in the tumor tissue itself. The diet promoted the accumulation of immune cells, which in the past have been associated with good chances of recovery and/or a better response to therapy. In addition, the researchers found that some of the immune system changes caused by the diet are long-term, lasting at least 40 days after the diet is stopped. This suggests that fasting-like diets could have a lasting impact on the immune system and increase the effectiveness of cancer treatments. These effects could be particularly useful in less advanced tumors or in combination with certain immunotherapies.
Taken together, these results suggest that the cyclic fasting-like diet represents a safe, feasible, and cost-effective nutritional intervention that modulates systemic metabolism and promotes the anticancer immune response in patients.
To date, there is no reliable data on the role of nutrition in Lynch patients and preventive nutritional recommendations are therefore lacking. However, epidemiological studies suggest that persistent inflammation in the intestine can promote the development and growth of adenomas and the development of colon cancer. These observations suggest that the effects of FMD on tumors and immune response described in mouse models and human studies, combined with intensive endoscopic surveillance, may help reduce the risk of new tumor formation and development in Lynch patients. Based on this hypothesis, the ANTIPASTO study will investigate the safety and feasibility of FMD as well as the effects on tumors and the immune system in patients with Lynch syndrome.

interventions.name:
FMD group: Patients with Lynch syndrome perform a fasting-mimicking diet (FMD). Following colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy as part of standard care, patients complete three 5-day FMD cycles spaced 28 days apart over 60 days.
The FMD is a reduced-calorie, low-carbohydrate and low-protein d
Control group: Patients with Lynch syndrome with a freely selectable, usual diet for 60 days after a colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopyas part of standard care.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Confirmed diagnosis of Lynch syndrome (pathogenic variant in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) 
• Age ≥18 years
• Willingness to follow a fasting diet per protocol and ability to swallow plant foods
• Body mass index (BMI) ≥20 kg/m2
• Written informed consent to participate in the study in accordance with the requirements of the local ethics committee
• Willingness to provide blood and urine samples and participate in endoscopic examinations as per protocol
• Willingness to put together and follow a diet
• Willingness and ability to remain in contact with study staff by telephone or email to communicate important clinical information, including daily body weight, blood pressure, health status, and adverse events on each of the five days of the diet
Exclusion criteria:
• Diagnosed with Crohn's disease, colitis ulecerosa, active diverculitis
• Active intestinal bleeding
• Unintentional weight loss ≥5% during the last 3-6 months
• Known HIV infection
• for women: existing or planned pregnancy (positive pregnancy test, e.g. β-HCG test in urine/serum/plasma) or breastfeeding
• Diagnosis of type I or type II diabetes mellitus requiring drug therapy
• Fasting glucose <65 mg/dL or >200 mg/dL
• Hemoglobin <9.0 g/dL
• Leukocyte values ​​outside the normal range
• Uric acid >7.0 mg/dl
• Impaired kidney function (GFR below the normal range)
• Impaired liver function (total bilirubin >2.0 mg/dl or AST/ALT 2 times ULN)
• After colectomy
• Known or ongoing abuse of medication, drugs or alcohol
• Concurrent participation in another clinical trial or participation in a clinical trial with an investigational drug up to 120 days prior to participation in this clinical trial
